newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka oil needs seen rising 12 pct in 1997 - CPC.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka oil needs seen rising 12 pct in 1997 - CPC.

text.p: Sri Lanka's oil products needs are expected to rise 12.5 percent to 2.7 million tonnes in calendar 1997, from an estimated 2.4 million this year, a senior official at Ceylon Petroleum Corporation (CPC) said on Thursday.
In 1995, Sri Lanka consumed 2.2 million tonnes of oil products.

D. Chandrasekera, manager at the state firm in charge of refining, told Reuters that demand for diesel and fuel oil would rise sharply as the country tried to raise thermal power generation to reduce dependence on hydropower.
Sri Lanka will need 245,000 tonnes of heavy diesel for thermal power generation in 1997, up from a projected 230,000 tonnes this year, he said.
The heavy diesel estimate for this year could rise because thermal power stations were running at full speed after drought reduced hydropower generation in the middle of the year, he added.
The Indian Ocean island has a power generating capacity of about 1,250 megawatts, 84 percent of which is from hydroelectric plants and the balance from thermal power plants.
The power crunch forced the government to impose daily power cuts of up to eight hours this year.
The state-run Ceylon Electricity Board has said it plans to build more thermal power plants to eventually reduce dependence on hydropower to 50 percent of the country's requirement.
Chandrasekera said his refinery, capable of processing 2.1 million tonnes of crude a year, can meet rising demand for fuel oil and petrol.
"But we'll have to import more diesel and Jet A1 aviation fuel," Chandrasekera said.
Sri Lanka's auto diesel consumption, which is about four times that of petrol, is forecast to rise to 970,000 tonnes in 1997 from an estimated 890,000 tonnes this year, he said.
Demand for petrol is forecast at 213,000 tonnes in 1997 from 200,000 tonnes this year, he said.
The refinery plans to raise petrol output to 270,000 tonnes by 1999 from this year's 200,000 tonnes, he said.
Chandrasekera said the state refinery had no immediate plans to raise the plant's overall capacity.
"We intend to modify the plant to reduce sulfer content in auto diesel for environmental reasons," Chandrasekera said.
The refinery will be shut down for six weeks from the middle of January till the end of February for maintenance during which imports of processed products will have to increase, he said.
